claim: Binary fission has been well studied in rod-shaped bacteria, but the mechanisms underlying cell division in spherical bacteria are poorly understood.
source: Binary fission has been well studied in rod-shaped bacteria, but the mechanisms underlying cell division in spherical bacteria are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by the general scientific consensus and the context of the study.

claim: Rod-shaped bacteria harbor regulatory proteins that place and remodel the division machinery during cytokinesis.
source: Rod-shaped bacteria harbor regulatory proteins that place and remodel the division machinery during cytokinesis.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about bacterial cell division in rod-shaped bacteria.

claim: The essential protein GpsB localizes to mid-cell during cell division in Staphylococcus aureus.
source: In the spherical human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus, we found that the essential protein GpsB localizes to mid-cell during cell division and co-constricts with the division machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data presented in the manuscript showing GpsB-GFP localization.

claim: GpsB co-constricts with the division machinery during cell division in S. aureus.
source: In the spherical human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus, we found that the essential protein GpsB localizes to mid-cell during cell division and co-constricts with the division machinery.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy and super-resolution imaging data showing GpsB following membrane constriction.

claim: Depletion of GpsB arrested cell division and led to cell lysis in S. aureus.
source: Depletion of GpsB arrested cell division and led to cell lysis, whereas overproduction of GpsB inhibited cell division and led to the formation of enlarged cells.
evidence: This is supported by antisense RNA depletion experiments and microscopy observations.

claim: Overproduction of GpsB inhibited cell division and led to the formation of enlarged cells in S. aureus.
source: Depletion of GpsB arrested cell division and led to cell lysis, whereas overproduction of GpsB inhibited cell division and led to the formation of enlarged cells.
evidence: This is supported by inducible overexpression experiments and cell size measurements.

claim: S. aureus GpsB directly interacts with the core divisome component FtsZ.
source: We report that S. aureus GpsB, unlike other Firmicutes GpsB orthologs, directly interacts with the core divisome component FtsZ.
evidence: This is supported by co-sedimentation assays showing GpsB pelleting with polymerized FtsZ.

claim: S. aureus GpsB interaction with FtsZ is unlike other Firmicutes GpsB orthologs.
source: We report that S. aureus GpsB, unlike other Firmicutes GpsB orthologs, directly interacts with the core divisome component FtsZ.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published literature on GpsB orthologs in other species and functional complementation experiments.

claim: GpsB bundles and organizes FtsZ filaments.
source: GpsB bundles and organizes FtsZ filaments and also stimulates the GTPase activity of FtsZ.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy showing bundled FtsZ filaments in the presence of GpsB and differential centrifugation assays.

claim: GpsB stimulates the GTPase activity of FtsZ.
source: GpsB bundles and organizes FtsZ filaments and also stimulates the GTPase activity of FtsZ.
evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assays showing increased phosphate release in the presence of GpsB.

claim: GpsB orchestrates the initial stabilization of the Z-ring at the onset of cell division.
source: We propose that GpsB orchestrates the initial stabilization of the Z-ring at the onset of cell division and participates in the subsequent remodeling of the divisome during cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of multiple experimental observations.

claim: GpsB participates in the remodeling of the divisome during cytokinesis.
source: We propose that GpsB orchestrates the initial stabilization of the Z-ring at the onset of cell division and participates in the subsequent remodeling of the divisome during cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the co-constriction behavior and GTPase stimulation activity.

claim: Bacterial cell division has been extensively studied in rod-shaped organisms such as Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis.
source: Bacterial cell division has been extensively studied in rod-shaped organisms such as Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis (Adams and Errington, 2009; Lutkenhaus et al., 2012; Rowlett and Margolin, 2015; Tsang and Bernhardt, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles on bacterial cell division.

claim: Spherical bacteria lack several key components found in rod-shaped model organisms.
source: However, spherical bacteria lack several key components found in these well-studied model organisms (Pinho et al., 2013), so fundamental features of how they divide are poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a comparative study of bacterial cell division components.

claim: Staphylococcus aureus is commensal in ~30% of the U.S. population.
source: The Gram-positive human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus is a spherical bacterium that is commensal in ~30% of the U.S. population (Kuehnert et al., 2006), but in immunocompromised individuals, it is a leading cause of bacteremia and nosocomial infections in industrialized nations (Klevens et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an epidemiological study.

claim: S. aureus is a leading cause of bacteremia and nosocomial infections in immunocompromised individuals in industrialized nations.
source: The Gram-positive human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus is a spherical bacterium that is commensal in ~30% of the U.S. population (Kuehnert et al., 2006), but in immunocompromised individuals, it is a leading cause of bacteremia and nosocomial infections in industrialized nations (Klevens et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a clinical study.

claim: Several antibiotic resistant strains of S. aureus have emerged.
source: The emergence of several antibiotic resistant strains of S. aureus has necessitated the identification of novel antibiotic targets (Pendleton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review on antibiotic resistance.

claim: Components of the bacterial cell division machinery have been proposed as antibiotic targets.
source: In recent years, components of the bacterial cell division machinery have been proposed as such targets (Lock and Harry, 2008; Sass and Brötz-Oesterhelt, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews on cell division as drug targets.

claim: GpsB is a small coiled-coil cell division protein.
source: GpsB is a small coiled-coil cell division protein (Claessen et al., 2008; Rismondo et al., 2016; Tavares et al., 2008) that is widely conserved in the Firmicutes phylum and is conditionally required for growth in certain species, depending on growth media and temperatures (Claessen et al., 2008; Fleurie et al., 2014; Land et al., 2013; Rismondo et al., 2016; Tavares et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and functional studies of GpsB.

claim: GpsB is widely conserved in the Firmicutes phylum.
source: GpsB is a small coiled-coil cell division protein (Claessen et al., 2008; Rismondo et al., 2016; Tavares et al., 2008) that is widely conserved in the Firmicutes phylum and is conditionally required for growth in certain species, depending on growth media and temperatures (Claessen et al., 2008; Fleurie et al., 2014; Land et al., 2013; Rismondo et al., 2016; Tavares et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative genomic studies.

claim: GpsB is conditionally required for growth in certain species, depending on growth media and temperatures.
source: GpsB is a small coiled-coil cell division protein (Claessen et al., 2008; Rismondo et al., 2016; Tavares et al., 2008) that is widely conserved in the Firmicutes phylum and is conditionally required for growth in certain species, depending on growth media and temperatures (Claessen et al., 2008; Fleurie et al., 2014; Land et al., 2013; Rismondo et al., 2016; Tavares et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies in various bacterial species.

claim: GpsB is highly co-conserved with the cell division protein DivIVA.
source: GpsB is highly co-conserved (Pinho et al., 2013) with the cell division protein DivIVA.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a comparative genomic study.

claim: GpsB harbors a highly homologous N-terminal α-helical domain similar to DivIVA.
source: Like DivIVA, GpsB is relatively small and harbors a highly homologous N-terminal α-helical domain.
evidence: This is based on structural comparisons and sequence alignments.

claim: The C-terminus of GpsB differs from that of DivIVA.
source: However, the C-terminus differs from that of DivIVA: whereas DivIVA assembles into an anti-parallel tetramer, the GpsB structure was reported to hexamerize with a parallel alignment of helices (Rismondo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a structural study of GpsB.

claim: DivIVA assembles into an anti-parallel tetramer.
source: However, the C-terminus differs from that of DivIVA: whereas DivIVA assembles into an anti-parallel tetramer, the GpsB structure was reported to hexamerize with a parallel alignment of helices (Rismondo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DivIVA structure.

claim: GpsB was reported to hexamerize with a parallel alignment of helices.
source: However, the C-terminus differs from that of DivIVA: whereas DivIVA assembles into an anti-parallel tetramer, the GpsB structure was reported to hexamerize with a parallel alignment of helices (Rismondo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a structural study.

claim: GpsB orthologs perform slightly different functions in different species.
source: Similar to DivIVA (Kaval and Halbedel, 2012), GpsB orthologs perform slightly different functions in different species.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and subsequent examples from different bacterial species.

claim: In B. subtilis and L. monocytogenes, GpsB participates in shuttling a cell wall assembly protein to help maintain the characteristic rod shape.
source: In the rod-shaped Bacillus subtilis and Listeria monocytogenes, GpsB participates in shuttling a cell wall assembly protein (PBP1 or PBP A1, respectively) to help maintain the characteristic rod shape of the bacterium (Claessen et al., 2008; Rismondo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies in these organisms.

claim: In S. pneumoniae, GpsB interacts with PBP2a, PBP2b, and MreC.
source: In the ovoid-shaped Streptococcus pneumoniae, GpsB additionally has been reported to interact with PBP2a, PBP2b, and MreC, and has been implicated in recruiting a Ser/Thr kinase to mid-cell that activates cell wall assembly machinery specifically at the division septum, thereby modulating a switch between peripheral and medial cell wall assembly to again maintain the proper shape of the cell (Fleurie et al., 2014; Rued et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in S. pneumoniae.

claim: In S. pneumoniae, GpsB has been implicated in recruiting a Ser/Thr kinase to mid-cell that activates cell wall assembly machinery at the division septum.
source: In the ovoid-shaped Streptococcus pneumoniae, GpsB additionally has been reported to interact with PBP2a, PBP2b, and MreC, and has been implicated in recruiting a Ser/Thr kinase to mid-cell that activates cell wall assembly machinery specifically at the division septum, thereby modulating a switch between peripheral and medial cell wall assembly to again maintain the proper shape of the cell (Fleurie et al., 2014; Rued et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: In all reported cases, GpsB interacts with a peripheral divisome component, EzrA.
source: In all reported cases, GpsB interacts with a peripheral divisome component, EzrA, but not necessarily core components of the division machinery, to mediate its role in cell shape maintenance (Claessen et al., 2008; Fleurie et al., 2014; Rued et al., 2017; Steele et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing GpsB-EzrA interactions.

claim: GpsB does not necessarily interact with core components of the division machinery in other reported cases.
source: In all reported cases, GpsB interacts with a peripheral divisome component, EzrA, but not necessarily core components of the division machinery, to mediate its role in cell shape maintenance (Claessen et al., 2008; Fleurie et al., 2014; Rued et al., 2017; Steele et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations and contrasts with the findings in S. aureus.

claim: In S. aureus, GpsB is an essential protein.
source: In S. aureus, GpsB is an essential protein (Santiago et al., 2015) (M. Santiago, personal communication), but its cellular function is poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and personal communication.

claim: Overproduction of S. aureus GpsB in B. subtilis causes a severe growth defect.
source: In the presence of inducer, otherwise WT B. subtilis harboring either gpsBSa or gpsBSa-GFP exhibited a severe growth defect (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by growth assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Overproduction of B. subtilis GpsB in B. subtilis does not cause a growth defect.
source: In contrast, cells similarly expressing gpsBBs or gpsBBs-GFP did not exhibit a growth defect (Figure 1A), suggesting that cell toxicity was specifically due to expression of the S. aureus ortholog of gpsB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by growth assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Overproduction of S. aureus GpsB results in approximately 3.2 fold overproduction at a population level in B. subtilis.
source: Immunoblotting with antisera specific to GpsBSa revealed a ~ 3.2 fold overproduction of GpsBSa at a population level in the presence of inducer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; note that the anti-GpsBSa antiserum did not recognize GpsBBs).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: B. subtilis cells overproducing S. aureus GpsB are filamentous with segregated chromosomes that rarely elaborate division septa.
source: In the absence of inducer, B. subtilis cells harboring gpsBSa examined by epifluorescence microscopy were of uniform length and displayed division septa at mid-cell (Figure 1B), but in the presence of inducer, these cells were filamentous with segregated chromosomes that rarely elaborated division septa (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Overproduction of S. aureus GpsB in B. subtilis deletion mutants of ezrA, ponA, prkC, gpsB, or divIVA results in filamentation.
source: Deletion of ezrA, ponA, prkC, or gpsB resulted in minor morphological defects in B. subtilis, but overproduction of GpsBSa in these strain backgrounds nonetheless resulted in filamentation (Figure 1D–K). Additionally, while deletion of divIVA resulted in cell elongation (Edwards and Errington, 1997), overproduction of GpsBSa in the absence of DivIVA resulted in further filamentation (Figure 1L–M).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 1D-M.

claim: The B. subtilis filamentation phenotype resulting from S. aureus GpsB overproduction does not require ezrA, ponA, prkC, gpsB, or divIVA.
source: Thus, the B. subtilis filamentation phenotype resulting from GpsBSa overproduction does not require these peripheral cell division factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of these genes does not prevent filamentation upon GpsB overproduction.

claim: Overproduction of S. aureus GpsB in B. subtilis causes diffuse localization of FtsZ-GFP in the cytosol.
source: In the absence of inducer, FtsZ-GFP localized properly to mid-cell at incipient and active sites of cell division (Figure 1N). However, upon overproduction of GpsBSa, filamentous cells displayed diffuse localization of FtsZ-GFP in the cytosol (Figure 1O), suggesting that GpsBSa overproduction interferes with the localization of the central component of the B. subtlis cell division machinery.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 1N-O.

claim: S. aureus GpsB was unable to complement the B. subtilis gpsB deletion phenotype.
source: In B. subtilis cells harboring a gpsB deletion and expressing gpsBBs, we obtained 865 ± 157 transformants harboring a deletion in ezrA (n = 3, per ~400 ng of transformed DNA containing ezrA deletion), whereas we did not recover any transformants when we attempted to delete ezrA in ∆gpsB cells that expressed gpsBSa, indicating that gpsBSa was unable to complement the gpsBBs deletion phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by transformation efficiency data.

claim: Overproduction of S. aureus GpsB in S. aureus results in approximately 5.4 fold overproduction at a population level.
source: Immunoblotting revealed an ~5.4 fold overproduction of GpsB at a population level relative to endogenous levels of GpsB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 56.9% of S. aureus cells overproducing GpsB are larger than 1.2 μm in diameter.
source: In the absence of inducer, 6.4% (n = 971) of cells harboring the inducible copy of gpsBSa were larger than 1.2 μm in diameter; in the presence of inducer, 56.9% (n = 770) of cells were larger than 1.2 μm (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is supported by cell size measurements and microscopy shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Overproduction of B. subtilis GpsB does not result in enlargement of S. aureus cells.
source: Interestingly, overproduction of gpsBBs did not result in a similar enlargement of S. aureus cells (Figure 2G–H), suggesting that the cell division inhibition phenotype in B. subtilis and S. aureus was unique to the overproduction of the S. aureus ortholog of GpsB.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and cell size measurements shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: Cells depleted of GpsB that had already elaborated a division septum did not complete cytokinesis.
source: At later time points, we observed that cells harboring the depletion construct that had already elaborated a division septum (Figure 2L, arrow) did not complete cytokinesis. Instead, the division septa became deformed and membrane aberrantly accumulated as foci.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Cells depleted of GpsB that had not yet initiated cell division did not elaborate division septa and accumulated aberrant membrane foci.
source: Cells that had not yet initiated cell division at the time of induction (Figure 2L, arrowhead) did not elaborate division septa and also accumulated aberrant membrane foci.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 2L.

claim: A suppressor mutation L35S in S. aureus GpsB corrects the growth defect caused by overproduction in B. subtilis.
source: One such mutation, an intragenic single nucleotide change in gpsBSa, altered the specificity of a highly conserved codon at position 35 from Leu to Ser (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, boxed residue), and allowed B. subtilis cells overexpressing gpsBSa-L35S to grow normally.
evidence: This is supported by genetic analysis and growth assays.

claim: The L35S substitution does not grossly affect the secondary structure of S. aureus GpsB.
source: The CD spectrum revealed similar profiles for each protein, suggesting that the L35S substitution did not grossly affect the secondary structure of GpsBSa.
evidence: This is supported by circular dichroism spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: S. aureus cells harboring inducible gpsBSa-L35S do not exhibit a cell enlargement defect.
source: In the presence of inducer, S. aureus cells harboring inducible gpsBSa-L35S did not exhibit a cell enlargement defect (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy shown in Figure 2I-J.

claim: GpsB-GFP localizes near the cell periphery in non-dividing S. aureus cells.
source: In non-dividing cells GpsBSa-GFP (produced at lower levels that did not result in cell division inhibition) localized near the cell periphery (Figure 3A, arrowhead).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy shown in Figure 3A.

claim: GpsB-GFP localizes to mid-cell and co-localizes with the constricting membrane in dividing S. aureus cells.
source: In dividing cells, GpsBSa-GFP localized to mid-cell, between the segregated chromosomes, and co-localized with the constricting membrane (Figure 3A, arrow).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy shown in Figure 3A.

claim: GpsB-L35S-GFP localizes primarily in the cytosol in both dividing and non-dividing S. aureus cells.
source: In contrast, GpsBSa-L35S-GFP localized primarily in the cytosol in both dividing and non-dividing cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy shown in Figure 3A.

claim: S. aureus GpsB-GFP is detected exclusively in the soluble fraction.
source: Unlike L. monocytogenes GpsB, we detected S. aureus GpsB-GFP exclusively in the soluble fraction, suggesting that it does not directly associate with the Staphylococcal membrane.
evidence: This is supported by cell fractionation and immunoblotting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: S. aureus GpsB is likely not directly membrane-associated.
source: We conclude that, unlike L. monocytogenes GpsB, S. aureus GpsB (hereafter, simply 'GpsB') is likely not directly membrane-associated and that cell peripheral localization of S. aureus GpsB may be mediated by another factor.
evidence: This is inferred from the fractionation data and comparison with L. monocytogenes GpsB.

claim: At the onset of cell division, GpsB-GFP forms an irregular ring-shaped structure in S. aureus.
source: At the onset of cell division, mid-plane images of S. aureus cells displayed only two GpsB-GFP foci that co-localized with sites of membrane invagination at mid-cell (Figure 3Bi). Reconstruction of deconvolved Z-stacks and rotation of the reconstructed image around the axis of cell division revealed that GpsB-GFP formed an irregular ring-shaped structure, reminiscent of the structure of an assembling divisome (Figure 3Bi) (Lund et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by structured illumination microscopy shown in Figure 3Bi.

claim: The GpsB-GFP ring structure co-constricts with the division machinery in S. aureus.
source: In cells that were further advanced in cell division, the two foci of GpsB-GFP followed the leading edges of the constricting membrane (Figure 3Bii) and formed a ring structure that was smaller than the diameter of the cell, (Figure 3Bii) (Buss et al., 2015; Ebersbach et al., 2008), suggesting that the GpsB ring structure co-constricts with the division machinery.
evidence: This is supported by structured illumination microscopy shown in Figure 3Bii.

claim: GpsB-GFP collapses into a single focus at the center of the invaginating membrane in cells approaching completion of cytokinesis.
source: In a cell approaching completion of cytokinesis, GpsB-GFP collapsed into a single focus at the center of the invaginating membrane (Figure 3Biii), and immediately after the completion of cell division, we observed that GpsB-GFP localized largely to the cell periphery in the adjacent daughter cells (Figure 3Biv), suggesting that GpsB may dynamically localize during the cell cycle.
evidence: This is supported by structured illumination microscopy shown in Figure 3Biii.

claim: GpsB dynamically localizes during the cell cycle in S. aureus.
source: To test the dynamic nature of GpsB-GFP localization, we followed the fate of GpsB-GFP in individual cells through three rounds of cell division using diffraction-limited epifluorescence microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 3C.

claim: GpsB localization to mid-cell depends directly or indirectly on functional FtsZ.
source: In the absence of inhibitor, GpsB-GFP localized at mid-cell or the periphery in 55% or 30% of cells, respectively, and mis-localized in the cytosol in 15% of cells (n = 200; Figure 4E–E'). In contrast, in the presence of inhibitor, GpsB did not localize to mid-cell in any cell observed (n = 200) and instead displayed a combination of diffuse cytosolic localization and aggregation along the cell periphery (Figure 4F–F'). The data therefore indicated that that GpsB localization to mid-cell depends directly or indirectly on functional FtsZ.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy with FtsZ inhibitor PC190723 shown in Figure 4E-F'.

claim: Overproduction of GpsB disrupts divisome assembly in S. aureus.
source: In otherwise wild type cells producing ZapA-GFP, no cell enlargement was detected; among them, 53% of cells displayed ZapA-GFP localized to mid-cell (these were cells that were actively undergoing cell division (Figure 4G–G', arrow) and 37% of cells displayed ZapA-GFP as a ring that corresponded to the subsequent plane of cell division in daughter cells that had recently completed cytokinesis (Figure 4G–G', arrowhead; n = 200). In contrast, in cells harboring inducible gpsB, addition of inducer resulted in the enlargement of cells and ZapA-GFP was mis-localized in 86% of the enlarged cells (n = 100; Figure 4H–I').
evidence: This is supported by microscopy of ZapA-GFP localization shown in Figure 4G-I'.

claim: Depletion of GpsB prevents robust divisome assembly at mid-cell in S. aureus.
source: In cells harboring empty vector, ZapA-GFP localized to mid-cell in 82.5% of the cells (n = 200; Figure 4J–J'). Quantification of fluorescence intensity in individual cells revealed that the fluorescence of mid-cell-localized ZapA-GFP was 2429 ± 1346 units/cell (n = 75). At earlier time points after induction to deplete GpsB, before cell lysis, we observed faint ZapA-GFP signals at mid-cell in 41% of the cells and diffuse localization in the remaining cells (n = 200; Figure 4K–K'), but the mean fluorescence intensity of the ZapA-GFP ring structure (614 ± 450 units/cell; n = 75) was nearly four-fold lower than that observed for ZapA-GFP intensity in the absence of gpsB depletion.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4J-K'.

claim: S. aureus GpsB elutes in two peaks by size exclusion chromatography, corresponding to hexameric and dodecameric forms.
source: GpsB eluted in two peaks by size exclusion chromatography, which approximately corresponds to the predicted sizes of hexameric (Rismondo et al., 2016) and dodecameric GpsB (Figure 5B, top), indicating that S. aureus GpsB could potentially exist in two forms.
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: GpsB-L35S elutes exclusively as a dodecamer by size exclusion chromatography.
source: In contrast, GpsBL35S eluted exclusively as a dodecamer (Figure 5B, bottom), suggesting that its inability to form hexamers could underlie its loss of function in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: S. aureus FtsZ hydrolyzed GTP poorly below ~30 μM.
source: Unlike the well-characterized E. coli FtsZ, which robustly hydrolyzes GTP (Arjes et al., 2015; Buske and Levin, 2012; Mukherjee and Lutkenhaus, 1998; Romberg and Levin, 2003), S. aureus FtsZ hydrolyzed GTP poorly below ~30 μM (Figure 5C) (Anderson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The rate of GTP hydrolysis by S. aureus FtsZ continued to increase with FtsZ concentration.
source: The rate of hydrolysis continued to increase with FtsZ concentration (Figure 5D), displaying a behavior more similar to FtsZ from the Gram-positive Streptococcus pneumoniae, which has a critical concentration above 10 µM, than to E. coli FtsZ (although a lag observed for S. pneumonia FtsZ was not detected for S. aureus FtsZ) (Salvarelli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis rate measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Incubation of 30 µM FtsZ with increasing amounts of GpsB resulted in a non-linear stimulation of GTP hydrolysis activity.
source: Incubation of 30 µM FtsZ with increasing amounts of GpsB resulted in a non-linear stimulation of GTP hydrolysis activity, wherein appreciable stimulation of GTP hydrolysis was only seen above 8 μM GpsB (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5E.

claim: At 10 µM GpsB, GTP hydrolysis by FtsZ was stimulated ~3 fold.
source: At 10 µM GpsB (1:3 ratio of monomeric GpsB:FtsZ; 1:18 ratio of hexameric GpsB:FtsZ; 1:36 ratio of dodecameric GpsB:FtsZ), GTP hydrolysis was stimulated ~3 fold.
evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5E.

claim: GpsB alone does not exhibit appreciable GTPase activity.
source: As a control, GpsB alone did not exhibit appreciable GTPase activity (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Incubation of FtsZ with GpsB-L35S did not appreciably stimulate GTPase activity of FtsZ.
source: In contrast, incubation of FtsZ with GpsBL35S did not appreciably stimulate GTPase activity of FtsZ (Figure 5F), nor did the addition of GpsB, even at equimolar amounts, to lower concentrations (10 µM) of FtsZ.
evidence: This is supported by GTP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Wild type GpsB stimulates the GTPase activity of FtsZ at substoichiometric levels at sufficiently high concentrations of FtsZ (above 30 μM).
source: Thus, wild type GpsB, which purifies as a hexamer and dodecamer, stimulates the GTPase activity of FtsZ at substoichiometric levels at sufficiently high enough concentrations of FtsZ (above 30 μM), whereas GpsBL35S, which is locked in the dodecameric form, fails to do so.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the GTP hydrolysis and size exclusion chromatography data.

claim: In the presence of GMPCPP, more than 50% of FtsZ was detected in the pellet fraction after ultracentrifugation.
source: In the absence of nucleotide, FtsZ was largely detected in the supernatant after ultracentrifugation, but in the presence of GMPCPP, more than 50% of FtsZ was detected in the pellet fraction, indicating that it had polymerized (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by co-sedimentation assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 94% of GpsB co-sedimented with FtsZ in the presence of GMPCPP.
source: When GpsB was incubated with the reaction, 94% of GpsB co-sedimented with FtsZ, whereas only 20% of the nonfunctional GpsBL35S co-sedimented with FtsZ.
evidence: This is supported by co-sedimentation assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Only 20% of GpsB-L35S co-sedimented with FtsZ in the presence of GMPCPP.
source: When GpsB was incubated with the reaction, 94% of GpsB co-sedimented with FtsZ, whereas only 20% of the nonfunctional GpsBL35S co-sedimented with FtsZ.
evidence: This is supported by co-sedimentation assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the absence of FtsZ, GpsB and GpsB-L35S were largely soluble.
source: Finally, in the absence of FtsZ, GpsB and GpsBL35S were largely soluble, suggesting that GpsB, but not GpsBL35S, interacts with FtsZ polymers.
evidence: This is supported by co-sedimentation assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Addition of GpsB increased the fraction of FtsZ in the pellet at slower centrifugation speed.
source: At a slower centrifugation speed, we detected 43% of FtsZ in the pellet fraction in the presence of GMPCPP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). Addition of GpsB increased the fraction of FtsZ in the pellet to 55%, whereas addition of GpsBL35S did not significantly alter the pelleted fraction of FtsZ.
evidence: This is supported by differential centrifugation assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the presence of GTP, FtsZ formed linear polymers ~100 nm in length.
source: In the presence of GTP, FtsZ formed linear polymers,~100 nm in length, that were abundant and scattered in different directions on the grid, indicating that it had polymerized successfully in a GTP-dependent manner (Figure 6D,H).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy shown in Figure 6D,H.

claim: In the presence of GpsB and GTP, FtsZ polymers formed long filaments closer to 1 µm in length that were oriented in a similar direction.
source: In the presence GpsB and GTP, however, FtsZ polymers formed long filaments, closer to 1 µm in length, which were oriented in a similar direction (Figure 6E,I). This pattern of orientation on an EM grid was reminiscent of the bundling behavior reported previously for proteins in E. coli that could promote lateral interactions between FtsZ filaments in vitro (Hale et al., 2000; Small et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy shown in Figure 6E,I.

claim: GpsB-mediated bundling of FtsZ did not require GTP hydrolysis.
source: With GMPCPP, FtsZ polymers were very long and in the presence of GpsB also exhibited extensive lateral interactions between FtsZ filaments, indicating that GpsB-mediated bundling of FtsZ did not require GTP hydrolysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy with GMPCPP shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Incubation of 10 µM or 20 µM purified S. aureus FtsZ with GTP did not result in an appreciable increase in light scattering.
source: Incubation of either 10 µM or 20 µM purified S. aureus FtsZ with GTP did not result in an appreciable increase in light scattering (Figure 6J), consistent with the apparent high critical concentration for FtsZ assembly suggested in GTP turnover experiments (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This is supported by light scattering assays shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Incubation of 30 µM or 40 µM FtsZ with GTP resulted in a rapid increase in light scattering followed by a brief plateau and then a decrease.
source: Incubation of 30 µM or 40 µM FtsZ with GTP resulted in a rapid increase in light scattering that likely corresponds to the assembly of FtsZ polymers. The increase was followed by a brief plateau, likely reflecting that the reaction was at steady state, then a decrease in light scattering, corresponding to disassembly of FtsZ polymers coincident with depletion of GTP in the reaction.
evidence: This is supported by light scattering assays shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Addition of 10 µM GpsB to the reaction with GTP and 30 µM FtsZ resulted in an initial increase in light scattering that was much more rapid and larger in amplitude than that of FtsZ alone.
source: Addition of 10 µM GpsB to the reaction with GTP and 30 µM FtsZ resulted in an initial increase in light scattering that was much more rapid and larger in amplitude than that of FtsZ alone in the presence of GTP (Figure 6K), whereas incubation of GpsB alone with GTP did not result in an increase in light scattering.
evidence: This is supported by light scattering assays shown in Figure 6K.

claim: The assembly of the higher order FtsZ structures generated in the presence of GpsB was reversible.
source: After reaching a plateau, the reaction containing WT GpsB displayed a steady decrease in light scattering, suggesting that the assembly of the higher order FtsZ structures generated in the presence of GpsB was reversible, in contrast to the behavior of other FtsZ bundling proteins reported in other systems.
evidence: This is supported by extended light scattering assays shown in Figure 6L.

claim: GpsB directly interacts with polymerized FtsZ and bundles FtsZ filaments.
source: We therefore conclude that GpsB directly interacts with polymerized FtsZ and bundles FtsZ filaments.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on co-sedimentation, electron microscopy, and light scattering data.

claim: FtsZ bundling by GpsB increases FtsZ local concentration and triggers GTP hydrolysis.
source: Taken together with the observation that GpsB also triggers GTP hydrolysis by FtsZ, we propose that FtsZ bundling by GpsB increases FtsZ local concentration and triggers GTP hydrolysis which, in the light scattering assay, is linked to the disassembly of FtsZ polymers as GTP is depleted.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on integration of multiple experimental observations.

claim: Cell division in S. aureus proceeds in two principal steps: an initial FtsZ treadmilling-dependent step followed by recruitment of peptidoglycan remodeling enzymes.
source: A recent report suggested that cell division in S. aureus proceeds in two principal steps: an initial FtsZ treadmilling-dependent step in which membrane invagination initiates, followed by recruitment of peptidoglycan remodeling enzymes by later arriving divisome components that mediates the progression and completion of cell division (Monteiro et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: GpsB may participate in the initial step that stabilizes FtsZ at mid-cell and activates GTP hydrolysis to trigger FtsZ treadmilling.
source: We propose that GpsB may participate in the initial step that stabilizes FtsZ at mid-cell and activates GTP hydrolysis (by increasing the local concentration of FtsZ via a bundling-like mechanism) to trigger FtsZ treadmilling, which is linked to constriction of the membrane and concurrent peptidoglycan synthesis (Bisson-Filho et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Intracellular levels of FtsZ and GpsB in S. aureus are approximately 4452 and 1659 molecules per cell, respectively.
source: Intracellular levels of FtsZ and GpsB are reported to be approximately 4452 and 1659 molecules per cell, respectively (Zühlke et al., 2016) (S. Fuchs, personal communication).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and personal communication.

claim: Considering a cell diameter of 0.8 µm, intracellular concentrations of FtsZ and GpsB equate to 28 uM and 10 uM, respectively.
source: Considering a cell diameter of 0.8 µm, this equates to intracellular concentrations of 28 uM FtsZ and 10 uM GpsB and corresponds closely with our in vitro reaction conditions.
evidence: This is a calculation based on reported molecule numbers and cell dimensions.

claim: GpsB is a multimer that may harbor 6–12 binding sites per multimer to recruit and bridge multiple FtsZ proteins.
source: We show that GpsB is a multimer and propose that it may harbor 6–12 binding sites per multimer to recruit and bridge multiple FtsZ proteins.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the size exclusion chromatography data showing hexameric and dodecameric forms.

claim: The bridging of FtsZ filaments by GpsB serves to increase the local FtsZ concentration and enhances GTP hydrolysis.
source: We propose that the bridging of FtsZ filaments also serves to increase the local FtsZ concentration and enhances GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the bundling and GTPase stimulation data.

claim: GpsB is the first reported FtsZ regulatory protein that promotes both lateral interactions between FtsZ filaments while also stimulating GTP hydrolysis.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report of an FtsZ regulatory protein that promotes both lateral interactions between FtsZ filaments while also stimulating GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on comparison with known FtsZ regulators.

claim: FtsZ polymers and regulators appear poised at the threshold between assembly and disassembly, enabling tight control over the division process.
source: Furthermore, considering the intracellular concentrations of FtsZ and GpsB and what we have observed biochemically, FtsZ polymers and regulators appear poised at the threshold between assembly and disassembly, enabling tight control over the division process.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the biochemical data and intracellular concentrations.

claim: Overexpression of gpsB resulted in the enlargement of S. aureus cells, reminiscent of the phenotype caused by depletion of FtsZ.
source: First, overexpression of gpsB resulted in the enlargement of S. aureus cells, reminiscent of the phenotype caused by depletion of FtsZ (Pinho and Errington, 2003), likely due to increased FtsZ GTPase activity leading to the inability of FtsZ to polymerize and treadmill in a concerted fashion.
evidence: This is supported by cell size measurements and comparison with cited literature.

claim: Depletion of GpsB in S. aureus resulted in the arrest of cytokinesis and abrogation of initiation of cell division.
source: Second, depletion of GpsB in S. aureus resulted in the arrest of cytokinesis and abrogation of initiation of cell division.
evidence: This is supported by antisense RNA depletion experiments and microscopy.

claim: GpsB co-localized with the cell division machinery at the onset of cytokinesis and co-constricted with the invaginating membrane during cell division.
source: Third, we observed that GpsB co-localized with the cell division machinery at the onset of cytokinesis, and co-constricted with the invaginating membrane during cell division, consistent with its role in modulating the activity of FtsZ.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing GpsB localization dynamics.

claim: Purified GpsB directly interacted with FtsZ in vitro and stimulated the GTPase activity of FtsZ.
source: Fourth, we found that purified GpsB directly interacted with FtsZ in vitro and stimulated the GTPase activity of FtsZ, consistent with the ability of GpsB to inhibit cell division in vivo when overproduced.
evidence: This is supported by co-sedimentation and GTP hydrolysis assays.

claim: When incubated with FtsZ in vitro, GpsB promoted lateral interactions between FtsZ polymers but also allowed for the ultimate disassembly of FtsZ once GTP had been depleted.
source: Finally, when incubated with FtsZ in vitro, GpsB promoted lateral interactions between FtsZ polymers, but also allowed for the ultimate disassembly of FtsZ in vitro once GTP had been depleted.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and light scattering assays.

claim: Staphylococcal FtsZ begins assembling at mid-cell and recruits GpsB to that location.
source: Our genetic, cytological, and biochemical data in sum suggest a model in which Staphylococcal FtsZ begins assembling at mid-cell and recruits GpsB to that location (Figure 7B) where GpsB stabilizes the Z-ring via a bundling-like mechanism that concentrates and organizes FtsZ polymers.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on integration of multiple experimental observations and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: GpsB stabilizes the Z-ring via a bundling-like mechanism that concentrates and organizes FtsZ polymers.
source: Our genetic, cytological, and biochemical data in sum suggest a model in which Staphylococcal FtsZ begins assembling at mid-cell and recruits GpsB to that location (Figure 7B) where GpsB stabilizes the Z-ring via a bundling-like mechanism that concentrates and organizes FtsZ polymers.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the bundling activity observed in vitro.

claim: GpsB reinforces the faithful and robust assembly of FtsZ at mid-cell at the onset of cell division.
source: We propose that this reinforces the faithful and robust assembly of FtsZ at mid-cell at the onset of cell division and drives an increase in the local concentration of FtsZ, which stimulates its GTPase activity, which is linked to treadmilling- an activity that is likely coincident with the initial membrane constriction that initiates cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: After completion of cytokinesis, GpsB redistributes to the cell periphery and awaits the next round of cell division.
source: After completion of cytokinesis, GpsB redistributes to the cell periphery and awaits the next round of cell division.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy showing dynamic localization.

claim: The dynamic redistribution of GpsB is presumably coincident with a dynamic ability to modulate FtsZ activity and may be dependent on the multimerization state of GpsB.
source: It is tempting to speculate that this dynamic redistribution of GpsB, presumably coincident with a dynamic ability to modulate FtsZ activity, is dependent on the multimerization state of GpsB.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed multimerization states and dynamic localization.

claim: The hexameric and dodecameric populations of purified GpsB could represent the active and inactive forms, respectively, of the protein.
source: In this way, the hexameric and dodecameric populations of purified GpsB could represent the active and inactive forms, respectively, of the protein that may mediate its interaction with FtsZ.
evidence: This is speculation based on the size exclusion chromatography data and functional differences.

claim: The inactive GpsB-L35S was locked in the dodecameric form and did not exhibit dynamic redistribution from the cell periphery to the cell division site in vivo.
source: Consistent with this model, the inactive GpsBL35S was locked in the dodecameric form and did not exhibit the dynamic redistribution from the cell periphery to the cell division site in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography and microscopy data.

claim: Depletion of EzrA, a known interaction partner of GpsB, also leads to cell enlargement.
source: Interestingly, depletion of a known interaction partner of GpsB, EzrA, also leads to cell enlargement, hinting at a possible collaboration between these two proteins in regulating cell division (Jorge et al., 2011; Steele et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on EzrA.

claim: Several divisome proteins in E. coli and B. subtilis that positively regulate cell division by bundling FtsZ polymers do so via inhibition of FtsZ GTPase activity.
source: Several divisome proteins in E. coli and B. subtilis that positively regulate cell division by bundling FtsZ polymers do so via inhibition of FtsZ GTPase activity (Durand-Heredia et al., 2011; Hale et al., 2011; Lutkenhaus et al., 2012; Mohammadi et al., 2009; Pacheco-Gómez et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2008; Small et al., 2007; Tsang and Bernhardt, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on FtsZ regulators.

claim: FtsZ bundling by GpsB is an intermediate step that increases local FtsZ concentration to stimulate GTP hydrolysis.
source: In our model, the seemingly contradictory observation that GpsB stimulates GTP hydrolysis, even though it promotes FtsZ bundling may be explained by the proposition that FtsZ bundling is not the ultimate activity of GpsB. Rather, we envision that FtsZ bundling is an intermediate step that increases local FtsZ concentration to stimulate GTP hydrolysis (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic model shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In E. coli, FtsZ polymers bundled by other proteins require FtsA to disrupt the bundles and destabilize FtsZ polymers.
source: This set of opposing activities exhibited in S. aureus in a single protein is reminiscent of the model in E. coli, where FtsZ polymers bundled by other proteins require a separate protein, FtsA, that can disrupt the bundles and destabilize FtsZ polymers (Conti et al., 2018; Krupka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on E. coli FtsZ regulation.

claim: FtsZ bundling in B. subtilis requires C-terminal positively charged residues.
source: In a slight variation of this model, since FtsZ bundling in B. subtilis requires C-terminal positively charged residues (Buske and Levin, 2012), it is conceivable that GpsB modulates exposure of the C-terminus of FtsZ to promote FtsZ self-interactions or remodels FtsZ to stabilize a conformation associated with enhanced GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on B. subtilis FtsZ.

claim: GpsB may orchestrate the organization, stabilization, and activity of FtsZ to remodel the divisome during cell division.
source: In this way, GpsB, an essential S. aureus protein, may orchestrate the organization, stabilization, and activity of FtsZ to remodel the divisome during cell division.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the proposed model.
